ex.d: Fill the three bands, one with each pen. Stagger the rows like bricks, keep the width constant, and lift the hand quickly at the end of each dash.
ex.c: the three bands read as the same gray from a distance and only the grain size changes.

ex.d: Touch and lift, without turning the tip. The space between dots equals the size of a dot.
ex.c: no dot has turned into a comma.

ex.d: A short hook that rises and falls to one side. Make them in groups of four or five that open like a fan.
ex.c: the tufts look like grass, not rain.

ex.d: Parallel strokes, always from bottom to top, easing the pressure in the last third. Never go back and forth.
ex.c: every stroke has a dark start and a light end.

ex.d: A cursive letter "e" repeated without lifting the tip. It is his mark for hedges and brush.
ex.c: the loops in each band are all the same height.

ex.d: Two clearly different directions. The second layer goes only where you want dark.
ex.c: the diamonds between the lines are an even size.

ex.d: The pressure is identical in all five boxes. What changes is the distance between dots. Start with the two end boxes.
ex.c: with your eyes half closed, the five steps jump by equal amounts.

ex.d: The same scale, now with flat dashes. Compare it with the previous one: the grays have to match.
ex.c: box 3 of this scale has the same value as box 3 of the dots.

ex.d: Short hatching in one direction only. Tighten the lines, not your hand.
ex.c: the darkest box still shows paper between the lines.

ex.d: Sea and sand: dashes on one side, dots on the other. The border gets no line; it appears because the mark changes.
ex.c: the edge reads without any contour.

ex.d: Commas on one side, dashes on the other. Let the marks of the two zones touch at the border.
ex.c: no white corridor is left between the two textures.

ex.d: One mark per band. Start at the horizon with the finest tip and switch to thicker ones as you come down.
ex.c: turned upside down, the ground still recedes.

ex.t: La Crau: eight bands and a high horizon
ex.d: Horizon in the top eighth, sky left blank. The hedges are rows of dark loops between the bands. The house gives the scale.
ex.c: the largest mark is more than 8 times the size of the smallest.

ex.d: The sun is a disk in contour with two rings of rays. The near wheat is made of long strokes bent by the wind.
ex.c: the rays do not touch the horizon.

ex.d: Short distance: the whole sheet covered, with a scale ratio of only 3 to 4 times. Each flower bed has its own mark.
ex.c: nothing blurs together, even with no blank areas.

ex.t: Boat on the beach: three substances
ex.d: Hull in a heavy, broken contour, sand in dots that grow as they come closer, sea in tiny dashes. The sky stays empty.
ex.c: the hull stands out by line weight alone.

ex.d: The thatch is made of short dashes that follow the curve of the roof. The path gets sparse dots that fade into the distance. The brush is made of curls.
ex.c: the two roofs have marks of different sizes.

ex.d: Four bands of sea. Each dash has a slight belly, like a small wave. The sails are straight contour.
ex.c: the sea looks flat and deep at the same time.

ex.d: Use the model as a base and his work as a reference. Write the key in the corner before you start: which mark goes with each color of the painting.
ex.c: you can point to where the yellow, the green and the blue were.

ex.d: Loose wrist, whole arm. Neighboring lines run almost parallel and never cross.
ex.c: each band looks like rippling fabric.

ex.d: Each curl is a C of three parallel strokes that rises and rolls over. Alternate the side it rolls toward.
ex.c: the curls look like flames, not worms.

ex.d: Near the center the dashes turn; farther away they go back to running horizontally. No dash crosses another.
ex.c: the eye is pulled to the center even though nothing is drawn there.

ex.t: Two centers turning in opposite directions
ex.d: One turns clockwise, the other counterclockwise. Between them the flow makes an S. This is the structure of the 1889 sky.
ex.c: the S between the centers is clear.

ex.d: First draw the flow lines very lightly, then cover them with dashes. The dashes get shorter near the centers.
ex.c: you can follow a current with your finger from one edge to the other.

ex.d: Long lines that spread apart before the stone and close up after it. This is how his sky behaves around the moon and the cypresses.
ex.c: the lines crowd together above and below the circle.

ex.d: Now the flow has to pass between two bodies. Notice how it speeds up in the middle corridor.
ex.c: the corridor between the circles has the closest lines on the sheet.

ex.d: All the rays point to the center of the disk. They grow as they move out and sit in staggered rings.
ex.c: if you extend any ray with a ruler, it passes through the center.

ex.d: Two swirls, four small stars and one large one. Each star is an obstacle with its own ring. The hill below runs in long lines.
ex.c: sky and hill have different marks and the same movement.

ex.d: The stalks change slant from wave to wave, and that is what makes the field move. Three bands, three sizes.
ex.c: the field seems to move from left to right.

ex.d: Fill each hill with long lines that follow its own back. Where two hills meet, the directions collide.
ex.c: each hill has volume without any shading.

ex.d: All the furrows leave from the same point on the horizon. It is his way of pulling the eye into the distance. The dashes grow as they come toward you.
ex.c: with the sun covered by your finger, the eye still runs to the same point.

ex.d: No contour. Start at the base and work up. Pack the curls in the core and loosen them at the edges. The ground goes in long waves.
ex.c: the silhouette reads without any line around it.

ex.d: The big one with big curls, the small one with tiny curls. The difference in mark size is what separates the planes.
ex.c: the small cypress looks farther away, not just smaller.

ex.t: Olive tree: ropes, curls and waves
ex.d: The trunk is made of lines that twist like rope. The crown goes in loose curls with paper between them. The ground undulates.
ex.c: trunk, crown and ground have three marks and a single wind.

ex.d: The village is made only of straight, vertical dashes. Everything around it is curved. Draw the village first.
ex.c: with the village covered, the drawing loses its force.

ex.d: Cypress as a dark anchor on the left, sky in two swirls, moon with a ring, straight village, hill in long lines.
ex.c: the cypress is the densest black on the sheet and connects ground to sky.

ex.d: Study the model, then copy his work. Notice that in the original the curls in the core almost merge.
ex.c: the core is at least three times denser than the edges.

ex.t: Master study: Wheat Field with Cypresses
ex.d: Wheat in waves, cypresses in curls, clouds in large loops, mountain in long lines. Four substances in flow.
ex.c: the clouds and the wheat ripple at different scales.

ex.t: The eye: rings around the socket
ex.d: The dashes turn around the eye like water around a drain. The upper eyelid is the thickest line on the face.
ex.c: the eye looks sunk into its socket.

ex.t: Both eyes and the bridge of the nose
ex.d: Each eye has its own swirl. At the bridge of the nose the two flows meet and turn into strokes that run down.
ex.c: the two swirls turn as mirror images of each other.

ex.t: The nose: bridge, side and wing
ex.d: On the bridge the dashes run straight down. On the side they turn and follow the swirl of the eye. Around the tip they make an arc.
ex.c: the nose comes forward without any contour line on the bridge.

ex.d: The mustache radiates out and down from under the nose. The lips are flat dashes. The line between the lips is heavy contour.
ex.c: the mustache covers the upper lip without hiding it.

ex.d: Commas that start near the mouth and run down and out to the sides, fanning out to the edge of the chin.
ex.c: the commas all point away from the mouth.

ex.d: C-shaped arcs, one inside the other. Heavy contour only on the outer edge.
ex.c: the ear reads with fewer than thirty marks.

ex.d: On the forehead the dashes make wide arcs, like wrinkles. At the hairline they change direction and become locks of hair.
ex.c: the border between forehead and hair shows only through the change of direction.

ex.d: The shadow side gets marks set closer together, with the same pressure. The marks keep turning around the eye.
ex.c: the cheek has volume without any smudged area.

ex.t: Direction map: face from the front
ex.d: Before filling in, look at stage 2 and redraw only the flow lines on a separate sheet. Then fill in zone by zone.
ex.c: you can redraw the flow lines from memory.

ex.d: The far side of the face gets narrower. The center axis becomes a curve. The swirls around the eyes are still there.
ex.c: the far eye is narrower than the near one.

ex.t: Face from the front, no beard
ex.d: Five zones: hair, forehead, cheeks, neck, coat. The background stays empty.
ex.c: with the eyes covered, the head still has volume.

ex.t: Three-quarter view with beard, looking left
ex.d: Six zones. Beard in commas against skin in dashes: this change of mark is what separates the two.
ex.c: beard and skin stay distinct, even at the same value.

ex.t: Three-quarter view with beard, looking right
ex.d: The same face, mirrored. Your hand finds the opposite side awkward, which is why you practice it.
ex.c: the two portraits, side by side, are equally good.

ex.d: The light side gets half the marks. The shadow side gets all of them. The pressure does not change.
ex.c: you can tell where the light comes from.

ex.d: His other solution for skin: the dashes on the cheeks leave the center of the face like rays. Compare with exercise c12.
ex.c: you can say which of the two directions you prefer and why.

ex.d: Cap in flat dashes, beard in commas, coat in cross-hatching, background in a lattice. The skin is the lightest zone.
ex.c: with the face covered by your hand, you can tell what each part is made of.

ex.d: The brim is made of dashes that go around the hat. The dotted background is calmer than everything else.
ex.c: the brim looks round, not flat.

ex.t: Young face, no beard, empty background
ex.d: Few marks. The skin almost blank on the light side, heavy contours on the eyes, nose and mouth.
ex.c: the face is resolved in fewer than three hundred marks.

ex.d: Alternating blocks of vertical and horizontal strokes, like basketwork. Lighter and more regular than the figure.
ex.c: the head comes forward from the background.

ex.d: Dashes that all point to the center of the head. A background that pushes the eye inward.
ex.c: the background does not compete with the face.

ex.d: The same face with marks one and a half times larger. Fewer marks, each one more decisive.
ex.c: the portrait works from ten feet away.

ex.d: The same face with marks half the size. The direction of each zone has to stay readable.
ex.c: up close, the zones still have different directions.

ex.d: Study the model, then copy his work. Start with the eyes and the cap, then the beard, then the coat. The background comes last.
ex.c: the background is lighter than the coat.

ex.t: Someone close to you, from a photo
ex.d: Study this model, then do the same with a photo of someone close to you: upload the photo in the Atelier to get its guide. Write the key in the corner: skin, hair, fabric, background.
ex.c: people who know the person recognize them.

ex.d: The background is made of dashes in rings around the head. Start with it and watch the head appear as an empty space.
ex.c: the rings are even and do not cross the face.

ex.d: On the crown the dashes make arcs that follow the dome. On the brim they go all the way around, like a racetrack.
ex.c: the brim and the crown have clearly different directions.

ex.d: Wide brim in dashes that go around, empty background. The hat takes up almost half the sheet.
ex.c: the brim casts a shadow on the forehead through mark density.

ex.d: In the Paris self-portraits, the dashes on the face leave the nose like rays and the background is dotted.
ex.c: face and background have marks of different sizes.

ex.d: Three centers in the background. The long lines flow around the head like water around a stone. Do the background before the face.
ex.c: the background moves and the face stays still.

ex.d: In 1889 the coat is made of the same waves as the background. Figure and background almost merge, and only the face holds out.
ex.c: coat and background look as if they were made of the same material.

ex.d: The eyes are the darkest, sharpest point. Heavy upper eyelid, iris as a solid dot, eyebrow in six short strokes.
ex.c: the gaze holds the sheet from ten feet away.

ex.t: Hair and beard: the same flame
ex.d: The hair rises and moves away from the face; the beard falls and moves away from the mouth. The two masses frame the skin.
ex.c: hair and beard have the same mark and opposite directions.

ex.d: A variation on the halo: the background dashes point toward the head. Compare with a01 and see which one gives more tension.
ex.c: you can explain the difference in effect between rings and rays.

ex.d: He painted himself sometimes turned to the left, sometimes to the right, because of the mirror. Do both and find your weak side.
ex.c: both are equally good.

ex.d: Very even dotted background, face in strong dashes. The opposite of the 1889 self-portrait.
ex.c: the face is the zone with the most energy on the sheet.

ex.d: Copy his work, translating each brushstroke into a dash, as in the model. Count how many different directions there are in the face alone.
ex.c: your copy has at least seven distinct directions in the face.

ex.d: Background first, then coat, then beard and hair, face last. In the face the marks get shorter and firmer.
ex.c: the face is the only still zone.

ex.d: In the mirror, or from a photo of yourself uploaded in the Atelier. Background in rings, as in the model.
ex.c: you recognize yourself.

ex.d: In the mirror. Decide where the three centers of the background go before you start.
ex.c: the background says something about your state of mind that day.

ex.d: Arm and leg are cylinders. The hatching goes around them like the hoops on a barrel. The shadow side gets rings set closer together.
ex.c: the three cylinders look round.

ex.d: Torso and coat are two barrels. The heavy contour goes only on the shadow side.
ex.c: the figure has weight on the ground.

ex.d: Back and skirt are two huge oval masses. The hatching changes direction with each mass.
ex.c: the back and the skirt have different hatching directions.

ex.d: Long stride, arm out, bag at the hip. The rings on each limb stay perpendicular to its axis.
ex.c: the figure seems to be moving.

ex.d: Torso tilted at 45 degrees, both arms on the spade. The weight goes onto the front leg.
ex.c: you can feel the effort in the back.

ex.d: The pose of Worn Out. With the face hidden, all the emotion is in the curve of the back.
ex.c: the figure looks tired even though the face cannot be seen.

ex.d: Study the model, then copy his work. On the leg, the hatching curves like the elastic of a sock.
ex.c: the leg looks cylindrical even with an almost uniform value.

ex.d: Study the model, then copy his work standing up, moving your arm from the shoulder.
ex.c: the hatching changes direction in at least six planes of the skirt.

ex.t: An open view of your neighborhood
ex.d: High horizon, five bands or more, sky left as reserved paper. The model is only a starting point for the composition.
ex.c: there is one mark per surface.

ex.t: A closed corner: backyard, garden, market
ex.d: A crowded sheet. Nothing blurs together.
ex.c: no area is left without a decision.

ex.d: No contour. Only curls, ropes and waves.
ex.c: the tree has a gesture.

ex.d: Flow lines, one straight element, a dark anchor.
ex.c: sky and ground have the same movement.

ex.t: Portrait of someone you know well
ex.d: Four substances, an active background, eyes as the darkest point.
ex.c: the person recognizes themselves.

ex.d: Choose the background that suits the day: halo, rays, swirl or dots.
ex.c: you would sign it.

sorrow.c: The Hague, April 1882. Pencil, pen and ink. The New Art Gallery Walsall.
sorrow.l: A single line, continuous and angular. The weight shifts: thick under the thigh and at the foot, thin where the light falls.

wornout.c: The Hague, November 1882. Pencil on watercolor paper. Van Gogh Museum.
wornout.l: The hatching on the trousers and sleeves goes around the form, like the hoops on a barrel.

orphan.t: Orphan Man with Broom and Pipe
orphan.l: The silhouette does all the work. Heavy clothes, big feet, no setting.

yard.c: The Hague, May 1882. Pencil, black chalk, pen and brush. Kröller-Müller Museum.
yard.l: Tile, plank, earth and laundry already get different treatments. This is the seed of the Arles alphabet.

peasant.l: Back and hips are two oval masses. The hatching runs in bundles that wrap around the volume.

reaper.l: The heavy contour sits entirely on the underside of the figure. The ground is a handful of scratches.

head85.t: Head of a Peasant Woman with Dark Cap
head85.l: Before the hatchings: the head as three masses of value. This is the volume the Arles marks will have to carry.

sower1.l: One of the many versions of Millet's theme. Long stride, arm out, the bag as a mass at the hip.

sower2.l: Huge feet and clogs. The visual weight stays low and plants the figure on the ground.

digger.l: The torso at 45 degrees and the two arms on the spade form a triangle. Compare it with the exercise guide.

lacrau.c: Arles, July 1888. Reed pen and fine pen, ink over graphite.
lacrau.l: The horizon sits near the top. The plain is a stack of bands, each field with its own mark, and the marks shrink until they become dots.

boats.t: Fishing Boats on the Beach at Saintes-Maries
boats.c: June 1888. Reed pen and ink over graphite.
boats.l: Firm contour on the hulls, sand in dots, sea in flat dashes. Each of the three substances gets its own mark.

street.c: Summer 1888. Reed pen and ink over graphite. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
street.l: Dotted thatch, an almost empty path, brush in loops. The sky is left blank.

garden.c: Arles, summer 1888. Reed pen and ink.
garden.l: The whole sheet is covered and nothing blurs together, because each flower bed has its own size and kind of mark.

harvest.t: The Harvest, drawing for Émile Bernard
harvest.c: Arles, July 1888. Pen and ink over graphite.
harvest.l: Made from the painting. The yellow of the wheat became a dash, the green became a comma, the fence became a comb.

rock.t: Rock of Montmajour with Pine Trees
rock.c: Arles, July 1888. Reed pen and ink over graphite.
rock.l: The rock is broken contour and short hatching. The pine crowns are made of loops, the brush below of commas.

stacks.l: Almost everything is dots and tiny dashes. The haystacks separate from the ground only through the direction of the mark.

arlesview.c: Arles, May 1888. Reed pen and ink.
arlesview.l: Foreground in large, loose marks, the town on the horizon in pinpoint dots.

cafe.c: Arles, September 1888. Reed pen and ink over pencil. Dallas Museum of Art.
cafe.l: The paving is made of dashes that converge toward the back. The stars are disks with rings.

cottages2.l: Thatched roof in dashes that run down, wall left blank, grass in commas.

starry.t: The Starry Night, drawing after the painting
starry.c: Saint-Rémy, June 1889. Pen and ink. It was in the Kunsthalle Bremen until the Second World War; today it is in the Shchusev State Museum of Architecture in Moscow.
starry.l: The dashes in the sky follow currents around the stars. The village is made of straight dashes. The cypress is the only dense mass.

cypress.c: Saint-Rémy, June 1889. Reed pen and ink over graphite.
cypress.l: The tree has no contour. Each curl is a C of two to four parallel strokes, always rising. The ground repeats the movement in long waves.

wheatcyp.l: Four substances in flow: clouds in large loops, mountain in long lines, wheat in short waves, cypress in flames.

wheatcyp2.l: The same composition in line. See how each color of the painting became a kind of mark.

fountain.t: Fountain in the Garden of the Asylum
fountain.c: Saint-Rémy, May 1889. Chalk, reed pen and ink. Van Gogh Museum.
fountain.l: The stones of the rim are dashes that go around. The trunks are made of lines that follow the twist.

olivep.l: The ground undulates in bands of short brushstrokes, all running the same way within each band. The trunks twist like rope.

enclosed.t: The Enclosed Field after the Storm
enclosed.l: The furrows converge on a point on the horizon and pull the eye into the distance.

pine.t: Pine Trees by the Asylum Wall
pine.l: Trunks in heavy contour, crowns in curls.

hands.l: Each hand is built as a box and five cylinders before any detail.

roulin.c: Arles, August 1888. Reed pen and quill, ink and black chalk. J. Paul Getty Museum.
roulin.l: Beard in curves that fan downward, coat in heavy cross-hatching, skin in dots and dashes, background in a lattice.

roulin2.c: Arles, August 1888. Pen and ink. Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
roulin2.l: Almost nothing but contour, plus hatching on the coat. The face and hands are left blank, with only a few strokes.

zouavepen.c: Arles, June 1888. Reed pen and ink.
zouavepen.l: The face in short dashes that follow the planes, the cap in dense hatching, the background in bricks.

escalier.l: On the face, the brushstrokes run down the cheek and circle the eyes. On the clothes, they run in vertical stripes.

escalier2.c: Arles, August 1888. Reed pen and ink. Harvard Art Museums.
escalier2.l: The hat is left blank. The background is dotted all over and pushes the head forward.

mousme.l: A young face with almost no marks. Heavy contour on the eyes and hair, background in sparse dots.

mousme2.l: Blouse in stripes, skirt in dots. Two patterns get two marks, and the face between them is left blank.

gachet.c: Auvers, 1890. Etching, the only one he made.
gachet.l: The lines of the face ripple in the same direction as the lines of the background. It is the Saint-Rémy stroke applied to a portrait.

tanguy.l: The coat is made of parallel brushstrokes that follow the arms. Behind him are the Japanese prints he collected.

sp_felt.c: Paris, winter 1887 to 1888. Oil. Van Gogh Museum.
sp_felt.l: The background forms a halo of dashes around the head. On the face, they turn around the eyes and run down through the beard.

sp_felteye.t: Eye detail from the self-portrait of 1887 to 1888
sp_felteye.l: Each brushstroke is a separate dash. They form rings around the eye, and the upper eyelid is the darkest mark.

sp_chi.c: Paris, spring 1887. Oil on cardboard. Art Institute of Chicago.
sp_chi.l: Dotted background, coat in diagonal dashes, face in dashes radiating from the nose.

sp_close.l: Look at the relative size: the dashes on the face are half as long as the dots in the background.

sp_straw.c: Paris, 1887. Oil. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
sp_straw.l: The brim of the hat is made of brushstrokes that go around. The background is short hatching in every direction.

sp_painter.c: Paris, winter 1887 to 1888. Oil. Van Gogh Museum.
sp_painter.l: The blue coat is made of short vertical dashes. The face uses smaller, more varied marks.

sp_gauguin.c: Arles, September 1888. Oil. Harvard Art Museums.
sp_gauguin.l: Calm background, almost flat. All the energy is in the planes of the face and the heavy contour.

sp_ear.c: Arles, January 1889. Oil. The Courtauld, London.
sp_ear.l: The coat in long parallel brushstrokes that follow the sleeve. The fur cap in short, bristling marks.

sp_orsay.l: The background is moving water and the coat joins the same current. Only the face stays still.

roulin2.inst: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (M.49.17.1)
